666.title: Janus looks both ways
666.hook: the Romans named January for Janus, who looks backward and forward
666.howItsDone: Some people mark a new year or a transition by deliberately looking back at what they learned and forward to one clear step, then returning attention to the present.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was new year, and Seneca's first letter. Your line was begin now: one hour, held, today.

Stand in a doorway for a moment. Behind you, the room you're leaving. In front, the room you're walking into. For a second you're in neither, and you can see both. Ancient Romans gave that spot its own god. His name was Janus, and on coins and statues he has two faces, one looking back and one looking forward. The doorway, the gate and the first day of the year all belonged to him. Our word January still carries his name.
screen: `STANDING IN A DOORWAY.` → `TWO FACES, BACK AND FORWARD.` → `JANUARY: JANUS'S MONTH.`

segments.voice: First, who he was to the Romans. Janus was the god of beginnings and passages: doors, gates, the start of things. In Roman worship his name was often called first in prayers, before other gods, because he stood at the opening. The poet Ovid, in his poem on the Roman calendar, has Janus explain his two faces like a doorkeeper who watches both the street and the house. Second, a famous door. In Rome, the gates of a small shrine to Janus stood open in wartime and closed in peace. They were rarely closed; the emperor Augustus boasted that they'd been shut three times in his rule. Third, what a Stoic would make of two faces. Seneca observes that fear and hope march together, and both come from a mind that leans ahead instead of standing in the present. Marcus reminds himself that the only life anyone loses is the moment they're living now. So a Stoic might say: look both ways, yes, but don't move into either room. Fourth, looking well. Look back to learn, not to replay: what went right, what would you do differently? Look forward to prepare, not to worry: what's one thing to do next? Then step through into the room that's real, which is this one. Janus himself stands in the threshold, after all, not in the past or the future.

segments.voice: Stand in a real doorway if you can, or picture one. Look back over the last few months for one thing you learned, then turn and look forward for one small, clear thing you want to do. Then come back to the doorway itself and feel your feet on the threshold, the only place you ever actually stand.
Janus, the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, with one face to the past and one to the future, who gave January its name. Today's word.
Your line: both ways. A glance back, a glance ahead, and then the room you're in. Day six hundred sixty-six.

667.title: The spring equinox
667.hook: day and night equal: an image of balance
667.howItsDone: Many cultures mark the spring equinox with new-year or spring festivals; some people use it as a moment to look at the balance of work, rest and company in their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Janus, the god in the doorway, one face back and one forward. Your line was both ways.

Twice a year, the sun, as seen from Earth, crosses the line of the equator, and for a day the whole planet, from Oslo to Cape Town, gets roughly the same amount of light and dark. Twelve hours, give or take. In March, for the northern half of the world, the light is winning from here on. Many peoples have marked it: Nowruz, the Persian new year, begins at that moment, and the date of Easter is still reckoned from a spring equinox fixed at March 21. Today the porch looks at the spring equinox as a picture of balance.
screen: `THE SUN CROSSES THE EQUATOR.` → `TWELVE HOURS, GIVE OR TAKE.` → `A PICTURE OF BALANCE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Equinox comes from Latin, aequinoctium: equal night. And a small surprise: it isn't exactly equal. Because the sun is a disk, not a point, and the air bends its light, most places get a few minutes more day than night on the equinox itself; the truly equal day comes a little before it in spring. Balance in nature is close, not perfect. Second, the Stoic picture. Seneca, writing to his friend Serenus about peace of mind, lists alternations. Mix solitude and company: being alone makes us long for people, people make us long to be alone, and each cures the other. Give the mind rest, the way you'd let a field lie fallow, because ground forced to produce every year wears out. He mentions that Socrates wasn't ashamed to play with small children. Third, what balance isn't. It isn't a perfect fifty-fifty schedule, like the equinox that's never quite exact. It's noticing which way you've tipped: too much work, not enough rest; too many people, not enough quiet; too much screen, not enough sky. Fourth, why spring is a good time to check. Things are about to grow fast. Days lengthen. Plans multiply. Before the light runs away with you, the equinox stands still for a day and shows you what even looks like.

See which side hangs lower, without scolding yourself, and choose one small thing to move across: ten minutes of quiet, a walk without your phone, a call to a friend if you've been alone too much. Picture the scale shifting, just slightly.
Aequinoctium, Latin for equal night, the root of the word equinox, when day and night come close to even. Today's word.
Your line: equal light. Close to even is as even as nature gets. Until tomorrow.

668.title: A neighbor's day of atonement
668.hook: Jews keep Yom Kippur as a day of fasting and repentance, in their own way and with their own meaning
668.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur many Jews fast from one evening until nightfall the next and spend much of the day in synagogue prayer; in the days before it, many seek out people they have wronged to apologize.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was aequinoctium, equal night, and a scale that's never perfectly even. Your line was equal light.

One autumn evening, synagogues fill for a day the Torah sets apart. Some people wear white. Those who keep the fast eat and drink nothing from that evening until the stars come out the next night, when a long blast of the ram's horn ends the day. This is Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Leviticus calls it a sabbath of solemn rest. It isn't ours to borrow. But a good neighbor can learn what it is, and let it ask a question of their own life.
screen: `AN AUTUMN EVENING, SYNAGOGUES FILL.` → `EVENING TO NIGHTFALL, NO FOOD OR WATER.` → `A NEIGHBOR'S HOLY DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the source. In the book of Leviticus, the tenth day of the seventh month is set apart. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, the people are told: "ye shall afflict your souls." Jewish tradition has long understood that as fasting and holding back from certain comforts, and the day is spent largely in prayer, from the evening service called Kol Nidre to the closing service, Neilah. Second, the inner work. At its center is the Hebrew word teshuvah, often translated repentance, though it comes from the root for returning. Turning back. Jewish teachers, Maimonides among them, describe recognizing a wrong, regretting it, setting it right where possible, and resolving to do differently. Third, other people. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish law, says Yom Kippur brings atonement for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs between one person and another, not until you've made peace with the person you wronged. So it's a custom, in the days before, to call, write and apologize. The day doesn't skip the phone call. Fourth, what a neighbor can take, carefully. Not the fast, the prayers or the meaning, which belong to the people who keep it. Only the question it leaves in the air for anyone watching with respect: have I looked honestly at my year? Is there someone I owe a word to? The Stoics had their own version, Seneca's nightly review, coming again soon. That's a different thing, from a different place, and it doesn't stand in for this one.
screen: `LEVITICUS: YE SHALL AFFLICT YOUR SOULS.` · `TESHUVAH: TURNING BACK.` · `WRONGED A PERSON? MAKE PEACE FIRST.` · `A NEIGHBOR'S QUESTION, NOT A BORROWING.` · then, large: `HONEST REVIEW.`

segments.voice: In your own way, look back over the past year, not to punish yourself, just to see: where you did well, and one place you fell short of who you meant to be. If a person is connected to it, picture them, and ask whether a word from you, an apology or a thank-you, might be owed. You don't have to decide now; just let the honest picture stand.
Teshuvah, the Hebrew word at the heart of Yom Kippur, meaning turning back: recognizing a wrong, regretting it, and resolving to do differently. Today's word.
Your line: honest review. An honest look comes before any setting right. Day six hundred sixty-eight, done.

669.title: The summer solstice
669.hook: the longest day, and Marcus would note it passes too
669.howItsDone: Many cultures mark midsummer with bonfires, outdoor gatherings or staying up through the short night; some readers of Marcus use the longest day as a reminder to enjoy what is passing.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was teshuvah, turning back, at the heart of a neighbor's holy day. Your line was honest review.

Nine-thirty at night, and it's still light enough to read on the back step. Kids are still out on bikes. Somebody's grill is still going. In the far north, in places like northern Norway, the sun doesn't set at all this time of year. The summer solstice: the longest day in the northern half of the world. People have lit bonfires for it, danced around poles for it, stayed up all night for it. The light seems like it could go on forever. Marcus Aurelius would enjoy it, and then gently remind himself of one thing.
screen: `STILL LIGHT AT NINE-THIRTY.` → `THE LONGEST DAY.` → `IT SEEMS TO GO ON FOREVER.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Solstice comes from Latin, solstitium: the sun standing still. For days around it, the sun seems to rise and set at almost the same points on the horizon, as if pausing at the top of its climb before turning back. Second, the pause is the turn. From tomorrow, in the north, the days begin to shorten, a little at a time. The peak of the light and the start of its going are the same moment. Third, Marcus. He writes that time is like a river made of things that happen, a strong current: as soon as something is seen, it's swept away, something else takes its place, and that too will be carried off. He tells himself to think often about how fast everything that exists is carried past and out of sight. To some readers that sounds bleak. But read beside his other notes, it isn't a reason to hold back from enjoying things. It's a reason to enjoy them now, while they're here, without trying to clamp them in place. Fourth, the solstice as practice. A long day can seem so roomy that it slips by unnoticed. Marcus's reminder turns that around: because it's passing, it's worth being out in. Both halves are true, and the second makes the first worth more.
screen: `SOLSTITIUM: THE SUN STANDING STILL.` · `THE PEAK IS ALSO THE TURN.` · `A RIVER OF THINGS, SWEPT PAST.` · `PASSING, SO WORTH BEING OUT IN.` · then, large: `LONG LIGHT, STILL PASSING.`

segments.voice: Go outside if you can, or sit by the window with the most sky, and look at the light as it is right now: its color, where the shadows fall, how warm or cool the air is. Enjoy it fully, without planning anything. Then notice, quietly, that this exact light is already moving across the wall, the ground, your hand, and enjoy it anyway, partly because it's passing.
Solstitium, Latin for the sun standing still, the root of solstice, the longest day when the light pauses before it turns. Today's word.
Your line: long light, still passing. The peak and the turn are one moment. That's day six hundred sixty-nine.

670.title: The ripe olive
670.hook: Marcus pictures an olive falling ripe, blessing the tree that bore it (Meditations 4.48)
670.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus use the image of the ripe olive to reflect on accepting life's seasons, and to eat food in season with attention and thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was solstitium, the sun standing still, the longest day already turning. Your line was long light, still passing.

If you've ever stood under an olive tree in the fall, in Greece or Italy or California, you might have seen it: fruit dropping on its own, a soft tap on the ground, then another. Nobody shook the branch. The olive was simply ready. Around the ancient Mediterranean, the olive was everywhere: food, lamp oil, medicine, the oil rubbed on athletes. And in book four of his notebook, at the end of a long, sober passage, Marcus reaches for one to say something hard in a gentle way.
screen: `A SOFT TAP ON THE GROUND.` → `FOOD, LAMPLIGHT, MEDICINE.` → `MARCUS REACHES FOR AN OLIVE.`

segments.voice: First, the long passage. Marcus lists people who are gone: doctors who frowned over many patients and then died themselves, astrologers who predicted others' deaths, philosophers who argued about immortality, great generals, whole cities. He isn't being morbid. He's reminding himself, again, how short and shared a human life is. Second, the olive. Then he turns. Pass through this little space of time in keeping with nature, he writes, and end the journey content, the way a ripe olive falls, blessing nature that produced it and thanking the tree it grew on. A falling olive doesn't cling. It doesn't curse the branch. It drops in its season, grateful. Third, what ripe means. For Marcus, everything in nature has its time: being young, growing up, getting gray, and also dying. Elsewhere he calls death one of the works of nature, like teething or a beard coming in. Some people find comfort in that; others find it hard. Both are honest reactions, and the Meditations don't demand that you feel one way about it. Fourth, the smaller lesson. The olive is in season: not early, not forced, not late, and it gives thanks for what grew it. Marcus means it as a way to end. It can also be a way to eat: a fruit picked in its own month carries the weather and the soil of the place it came from.
screen: `DOCTORS, GENERALS, WHOLE CITIES, GONE.` · `FALL LIKE A RIPE OLIVE, GRATEFUL.` · `EVERYTHING IN NATURE HAS ITS TIME.` · `IN SEASON: NOT EARLY, NOT LATE.` · then, large: `IN SEASON.`

segments.voice: Hold something in season, a piece of fruit, a vegetable, a handful of nuts, or picture one, and think of the plant it came from, the weather that ripened it, the hands that picked and carried it. If it's in front of you, taste it slowly. Let one silent thank-you go back to the tree, the field or the people, and sit with the taste.
Ripe olive, Marcus's picture of a life that ends in its season, falling without clinging, grateful to the tree that bore it. Today's word.

671.title: The autumn equinox
671.hook: balance again, and the light begins to shorten
671.howItsDone: Many cultures hold harvest festivals around the autumn equinox; some readers of the Stoics mark it with a dusk walk and a reflection on the seasons of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ripe olive, falling in its season and thanking the tree. Your line was in season.

It shows up first at dinner. In August, dinner was eaten in daylight. Now the kitchen light is on before the pasta's done. The mornings are cooler. The trees on your street have a few yellow leaves, like the first gray hairs. Back in the spring, the porch stood at the equinox and watched the light begin to win. Today the scale balances again, day and night nearly even. But this time, in the north, the dark grows. The autumn equinox: the same balance, facing the other way.
screen: `THE KITCHEN LIGHT, ON EARLIER.` → `A FEW YELLOW LEAVES.` → `THE SAME BALANCE, FACING THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Astronomically, it's the mirror of spring: the sun crosses the equator heading south, and northern days grow shorter than the nights. Some people feel it in their mood, a slight heaviness as evenings close in. That's real, and it's worth being gentle with. Second, Seneca in autumn. In his twelfth letter, he visits his country house and grumbles to the caretaker that the old plane trees look neglected. The caretaker says he's doing all he can; the trees are just old. Then Seneca remembers: he planted them himself. The trees are simply his age. And the letter turns: we should welcome and love old age, he says, because it is full of pleasure if you know how to use it. Fruit is most welcome when it's almost over. Third, turnings. For Seneca and Marcus, nature's cycles aren't something going wrong. Seasons turn, people age, the light comes and goes, and all of it belongs to the same whole. You don't have to like the shorter days. You can stop treating them as a mistake. Fourth, what autumn offers. The best light of the year, some say: low, gold, long shadows. Harvest. A slower pace. The turning isn't only loss. It's a different kind of day with its own gifts, the way the later part of a life has its own. Dusk shows it plainly, when day and night meet in the same sky.
screen: `THE MIRROR OF SPRING.` · `SENECA'S OLD PLANE TREES.` · `TURNINGS AREN'T MISTAKES.` · `A DIFFERENT DAY, WITH ITS OWN GIFTS.` · then, large: `THE TURNING.`

segments.voice: Watch the light go from a window or a doorway, or picture a dusk you remember: the colors draining from the sky, the sounds changing, the air cooling. Don't hurry it, and don't hold on to it. If a feeling of loss comes, let it be there; if rest comes, let that be there too.
Autumn equinox, when day and night return to balance but the light begins to shorten, a turning with its own gifts. Today's word.
Your line: the turning. Not a mistake, just the other face of the year. See you tomorrow.

672.title: Saturnalia, roles reversed
672.hook: the Roman midwinter festival turned roles upside down; Seneca stayed sober and practiced poverty (Letters 18)
672.howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca mark busy festive seasons by keeping a few plain days, and by giving thanks or gifts to the people who serve them through the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was autumn equinox, and Seneca meeting his own old trees. Your line was the turning. Today closes the week.

Rome, mid-December. The streets are loud. People have swapped their formal togas for loose, bright dinner clothes. Shops sell little clay figures and wax candles to give as presents. Gambling, usually frowned on, is allowed in public. In some households, ancient writers tell us, the strangest thing of all: for the feast, the enslaved people of the house are served, or sit at table with the family, and the masters wait on them. It's the Saturnalia, the festival of the god Saturn, and Seneca has some thoughts about how to spend it.
screen: `ROME, MID-DECEMBER.` → `CANDLES, CLAY FIGURES, DICE.` → `THE MASTERS SERVE.`

segments.voice: First, the festival. The Saturnalia began on December seventeenth and grew over time to several days. Romans remembered Saturn's reign as a golden age, before rich and poor, when everyone was equal. For a few days the festival played at that: freedom of speech, gifts, roles turned upside down. It was a game, and the next week everything went back. Rome was a slave society, and that should be said plainly. But the game admitted something: the order of things wasn't the only possible one. Second, Seneca's letter. It's December, he writes to Lucilius, and the whole city is sweating with celebration. Should we join in, or stay apart? Don't make a show of refusing, he says, but don't lose yourself. Keep a sober head while others are drunk. Third, his surprising suggestion. While everyone feasts, set aside a few days to live on the plainest, cheapest food, in rough clothing, and ask: is this what I was afraid of? Rich people sometimes did this for fun; he means it as training, so that poverty, if it came, would hold no terror. Fourth, the reversal that lasts. In another letter Seneca argues that the people who serve us are human beings like us, born of the same seed, under the same sky. A Stoic tries to keep a little of the festival all year: seeing the person who brings your coffee or delivers the box as fully a person. And a look back at the week: both ways. Equal light. Honest review. Long light, still passing. In season. The turning. Roles reversed.
screen: `SATURN'S GOLDEN AGE, PLAYED FOR DAYS.` · `SOBER WHILE THE CITY CELEBRATES.` · `PLAIN FOOD: IS THIS WHAT I FEARED?` · `THE PEOPLE WHO SERVE US ARE PEOPLE.` · then, large: `ROLES REVERSED.`

segments.voice: Picture someone who serves you in an ordinary week, the person at the counter, the driver, the cleaner, someone at home who does more than their share, and see their face clearly. Imagine the roles reversed, with you doing their work: how would you want to be treated? Let one small thing you could give them come to mind, a real thank-you, a kindness.
Saturnalia: the Roman midwinter festival when roles were reversed, and for Seneca a time to stay sober, practice simplicity, and remember who serves us. Today's word.
Your line: roles reversed. The one who serves is a person first. A week closed, and day six hundred seventy-two.
